questions.scenario: INV-8891 for $90,000 is invoiced on a B/L date. Which rate books the REVENUE entry?
options: Whatever rate the cash actually converts at, weeks later
The B/L-date transaction/booking rate
Month-end closing rate
Last year's average rate
questions.explanation: Original entries always use the EVENT-date rate — and for exports the event date is the B/L date (Module 6's recognition rule). Later rates only create FX differences.
wrongExplanations: Settlement rate creates the realized gain/loss later — it never rewrites revenue.
Closing rates revalue OPEN balances at month-end; they don't book new revenue.
Averages hide event-day reality; accounting translates events on their own dates.

questions.scenario: Booked receivable $90,000 @ ৳122.20. At settlement the bank credits @ ৳121.80. The ৳36,000 shortfall is:
options: Bank's error — demand it back
Nasrin's booking mistake
A REALIZED foreign exchange loss — taka strengthened between booking and settlement
Not recordable; ignore small differences
questions.explanation: Each dollar bought fewer taka at settlement than at booking → real economic loss vs the booked figure, recorded in FX Loss—Realized. Currency movement isn't anyone's error — but it IS always recorded.
wrongExplanations: Banks apply contracted rates correctly; the gap came from market movement over 60 days.
Booking used the correct B/L-date rate; nobody misquoted.
Unrecorded FX differences make bank reconciliations impossible — every paisa is explained.

questions.scenario: At month-end, H&M's receivable is still unpaid. Shirin revalues it at the closing rate, booking an unrealized FX gain. What is special about this gain?
options: It is permanent profit
It is recognized at the reporting date while the receivable remains unpaid; later rate movements create further FX differences
It must be paid to NBR immediately in cash
It belongs to the buyer
questions.explanation: Closing-rate revaluation changes the carrying amount. Settlement is compared with that latest amount; reversing prior adjustments is an optional workflow, not a universal requirement.
wrongExplanations: Only the SETTLEMENT difference is final; this one floats with the market.
Tax treatment follows tax rules (Module 14), not immediate cash payment of book gains.
It's Masco's accounting estimate of its own receivable.

options: Two buyers pay for the same shipment twice
Import LCs to suppliers are issued AGAINST the export LC's proceeds — raw materials financed by the confirmed export order
Paying suppliers before any order exists
An LC written on the back of the invoice paper
questions.explanation: It's the RMG financing engine: confirmed export LC in → bank issues matching import LCs out. It also naturally hedges currency: USD arrives to fund USD payments.
wrongExplanations: No double payment anywhere — one export finances its inputs.
Without a confirmed export, banks won't open these LCs — the linkage IS the product.
The name refers to linkage of instruments, not paperwork location.

questions.scenario: Why does Jamal's GRN accuracy matter to BOND license compliance?
options: Bond rules require pretty paperwork
Duty-free bonded imports must be proven to become exports, kg by kg (UD declarations); GRNs and issue slips are the evidence chain
They don't — customs ignores factories' records
Only the commercial team's documents count
questions.explanation: The bond privilege (duty-free imports) survives on traceability: imported yarn → production consumption → exported garments. Warehouse documents ARE that trail; gaps trigger duty recovery plus penalties.
wrongExplanations: It's a legal accountability regime, not aesthetics.
Customs and NBR audit exactly these records during bond audits.
Commercial documents start the chain; warehouse documents COMPLETE it.

questions.scenario: Bangladesh Bank's ~120-day export realization rule means:
options: Shipments must sail within 120 days of orders
Export proceeds must be realized within the regulatory window from shipment — overdue realization requires explanations and risks penalties
Employees get 120 days annual leave
LCs expire after 120 minutes
questions.explanation: Foreign receivable aging is REGULATORY, not just commercial. That's why the ERP's aging reports flag export invoices approaching the window — Nasrin chases documents, Shirin monitors the clock.
wrongExplanations: Production lead times are commercial matters; the rule concerns MONEY coming home.
Leave policy is HR's domain (though everyone would vote yes).
LC validity periods vary by terms — unrelated.

questions.scenario: Masco pays Chinese supplier $25,400. Booked @120.00, settled @121.50. The payable entry and FX direction are:
options: Dr AP $25,400×120 = 30,48,000 / Cr Bank same — no FX line ever
Dr AP 30,48,000 + Dr FX Loss—Realized 38,100 / Cr Bank 30,86,100 — paying MORE taka than booked is a loss on a payable
Cr Revenue 38,100 as compensation
Post nothing until year-end
questions.explanation: Payables move OPPOSITE to receivables: taka weakening against USD makes USD debts dearer. Kill the liability at booked value; the extra taka actually paid is realized FX loss.
wrongExplanations: Ignoring the 38,100 leaves the bank account unreconcilable by exactly that amount.
Revenue has no relationship to settling our own import debt.
Deferred recording breaks both month-end valuation and the bank reconciliation.

questions.scenario: Where do daily exchange RATES come from in a professional ERP?
options: Developers hardcode today's rate in Program.cs
Dated rate tables ingested from bank/Bangladesh Bank published sources — every FC entry stores amount, rate, and source document
Each accountant types whatever feels right
Rates are unnecessary — just use dollars everywhere
questions.explanation: Module 0's Golden Rule applies to rates: sourced, dated, auditable. Hardcoding violates change-control; free-typing invites 'convenient' rates; functional currency stays BDT regardless.
wrongExplanations: Hardcoded rates break silently when markets move — and audits ask 'source?'.
Free-typed rates are how fiction enters books.
Books remain BDT-functional even when trading in USD/EUR.

questions.scenario: Shirin notices export receivables aging past 90 days while the 120-day window looms. Best FIRST action set:
options: Delete the old invoices to reset aging
Escalate document/collection chase with commercial + inform bank relationship manager; check for disputes or document holds blocking realization
Book them as bad debts immediately
Convert the receivables into local sales retroactively
questions.explanation: Overdue export proceeds usually trace to stuck DOCUMENTS (amended B/Ls, discrepancy disputes), not vanished money. Fix the blocker before the regulatory window forces penalties.
wrongExplanations: Deleting records destroys the audit trail AND the receivable — fraud territory.
Bad-debt provisioning needs evidence of uncollectability, not impatience.
Rewriting trade history to dodge a clock is falsification.

questions.scenario: Rafiq must design the month-end close for FX. The correct sequence his job should automate:
options: Nothing — FX sorts itself out
Obtain sourced closing rates → revalue open foreign-currency monetary balances → record FX differences → reconcile balances and retain the calculation
Ask each buyer what they think their debt is worth
Revalue only profitable balances upward
questions.explanation: Use closing rates for monetary balances, preserve the reporting-period results, and reconcile each currency. Historical-cost non-monetary items do not all receive the same revaluation treatment.
wrongExplanations: Markets move daily; ignoring them misstates every FC balance.
Buyers owe CONTRACTED amounts; valuation is our books' job.
One-directional revaluation is selective truth-telling — the definition of bias.
